docs.title: tiny-langgraph
docs.text:
LangGraph-style AI agents for microcontrollers. Write the agent in Python like a LangGraph graph. tiny-langgraph turns it into C for an ESP32-S3 or a NodeMCU, where your rules and a planner decide, a verifier checks every action before it runs, and a web page served by the board shows the agent thinking, live.

Get started View on GitHub

Early (v0.4), research project

Runs on real ESP32-S3 and NodeMCU boards. Inspired by LangGraph; not affiliated with LangChain.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A big LLM can't come with you onto a $3 chip. But many devices only need to make good decisions in one narrow domain: a pet feeder, a door camera, a plant monitor. tiny-langgraph gives them the structure LangGraph gives LLM apps (a graph of steps, routing, loops, human approval) and makes every decision checkable:

  • your rules say what's wanted,
  • the planner finds the cheapest plan of tool calls,
  • the verifier checks it before anything runs,
  • a human approves anything you mark as risky.

docs.title: Thirty seconds of code
docs.text:
class Feeder(State):
    asked        = Choice("no", "yes")
    fed_recently = Choice("no", "yes")

goals = Goals(fed=Goal(5, only_if_wanted=True))

def may_feed(s: Feeder) -> bool:                    # checked on the device too
    return s.fed_recently == "no"

@tool(cost=3, achieves=goals.fed, needs=may_feed)
def dispense(s: Feeder):
    led.blink(3, 200)

@rules
def assess(s: Feeder):
    if s.asked == "yes":
        want(goals.fed)

python feeder.py                 # run it on your PC, hardware simulated
python feeder.py build nodemcu   # C code, checked against the Python, plus an Arduino sketch

The full agent is in Your first agent.

docs.title: What's in the box
docs.text:
• The LangGraph API you know

    StateGraph, add_node, add_conditional_edges, compile, invoke, interrupt, tools.

  • Python to C, checked

    Plain C11 with no heap in the graph runtime. The build stops unless the C decides exactly like your Python in every situation.

  • Safe by construction

    Rules, planner, verifier, and human approval with a PIN or a button.

  • Several boards

    ESP32-S3 and NodeMCU (ESP8266), built-in drivers, and your own C drivers.

  • Boards that talk

    Boards advertise what they can do and ask each other over ESP-NOW. The receiver's own rules decide.

  • MCP on the board

    AI clients such as Claude Code list and call a board's tools over Wi-Fi, still through its rules.

docs.title: Measured on hardware
docs.text:
ESP32-S3 NodeMCU (ESP8266) Plan + verify ~40 µs + ~37 µs ~120 µs + ~100 µs A tiny transformer instead of the planner ~120 ms, 185 KB flash, same answers doesn't fit Two boards over ESP-NOW watcher asks, feeder decides MCP call over Wi-Fi 0.3–0.5 s

More in Results and limitations.

docs.title: tiny-langgraph
docs.text:
LangGraph-style agents for microcontrollers: your rules decide, a verifier checks every action, and a tiny language model can optionally run on the chip.

Write your agent in Python, the way you'd write a LangGraph graph. tiny-langgraph turns it into C for devices like the ESP32-S3, where your rules and a planner decide what to do and a verifier makes sure nothing unsafe ever runs, offline. If you add a reason node, it also trains a tiny transformer on your rules and runs it inside the graph. A trace viewer shows the agent thinking, live, from the board's own web page.

Status: early (v0.4). Works end to end on a PC, and the pet watcher runs on a real ESP32-S3-CAM. The model is optional: for decisions that depend only on the current moment, rules + the planner are faster and just as accurate (see Results so far), so they're the default. Inspired by LangGraph; not affiliated with LangChain.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
A big LLM can't come with you onto a microcontroller. But many devices only need to make good decisions in one narrow domain: a door camera, a plant monitor, a machine watching for faults. tiny-langgraph gives them the same structure LangGraph gives LLM apps (a graph of steps, conditional routing, loops, human approval, checkpoints), and makes every decision checkable:

  • the planner proposes the cheapest plan for what your rules want (or, optionally, a small model proposes one and the planner repairs it if it's wrong),
  • the verifier checks it against your rules and conditions before anything runs,
  • a human approves anything you mark as risky.

docs.title: Write an agent in Python
docs.text:
If you know LangGraph, you already know most of it. This is the pet watcher (examples/pet_watcher/agent.py, abridged):

from tiny_langgraph import START, END, Choice, Think, Int, State, StateGraph, Goal, Goals, prebuilt, rules, tool, want
from tiny_langgraph.drivers import Buzzer, Clock, DigitalIn, Servo

counter = DigitalIn(pin=2)        # hardware, with your pins
buzzer  = Buzzer(pin=14)
feeder  = Servo(pin=47)
clock   = Clock()

class Pet(State):
    cat          = Choice("none", "seen", "in_zone")   # observed: the model reads it
    meal         = Choice("not_due", "due", "overdue")
    fed_recently = Choice("no", "yes")
    mischief     = Think("no", "yes")                  # concluded: the model predicts it
    fed_at       = Int(-1000)                          # memory, kept between runs

goals = Goals(recorded=1, deterred=Goal(4, only_if_wanted=True), fed=Goal(5, only_if_wanted=True))

def can_feed(s: Pet) -> bool:                       # a condition, checked on the device too
    return s.meal != "not_due" and s.fed_recently == "no"

@tool(cost=3, achieves=goals.fed, needs=can_feed)
def dispense(s: Pet):
    feeder.turn(90)
    s.fed_at = clock.minutes()

def sense(s: Pet):                                  # a node: plain Python
    s.cat = "in_zone" if counter.read() else "none"
    s.fed_recently = "yes" if clock.minutes() - s.fed_at < 180 else "no"

@rules                                              # the model learns these; the device checks it against them
def assess(s: Pet):
    s.mischief = "yes" if s.cat == "in_zone" else "no"
    want(goals.recorded)
    if s.meal != "not_due":
        want(goals.fed)

graph = StateGraph(Pet)
graph.add_node("sense", sense)
graph.add_node("assess", assess)
graph.add_node("plan", prebuilt.plan)               # the planner finds the cheapest plan
graph.add_node("verify", prebuilt.verify)           # checked against your rules and conditions
graph.add_node("ask", prebuilt.ask)                 # human approval for risky tools
graph.add_node("act", prebuilt.Act([log, chirp, dispense]))
graph.add_edge(START, "sense")
graph.add_edge("sense", "assess")
graph.add_edge("assess", "plan")                    # or: assess -> reason -> verify, to add the model
...
graph.add_conditional_edges("verify", prebuilt.after_verify, ["act", "ask", "plan"])
app = graph.compile(name="pet_watcher")

app.invoke(Pet(), verbose=True)                    # runs on your PC, hardware simulated

pip install -e .                  # from this repo (numpy, pyyaml; add torch to train)
cd examples/pet_watcher
python agent.py                   # try it on your PC
python agent.py build             # write C, check it, make the ESP32-S3 sketch
$env:USE_MODEL=1; python agent.py build   # the same with the model (PowerShell; USE_MODEL=1 ... on Linux/macOS)

app.build() (or python agent.py build) does everything between your file and the board:

Step What happens convert your nodes, routes, tools, conditions and rules become C (generated/) label every situation (3,888 here) is labeled by running your @rules and the planner train only with a reason node: the model is retrained when the rules or tools changed (~1.5 min on a laptop CPU) check the C is compiled and must decide exactly like your Python in every situation, or the build stops package build/pet_watcher/pet_watcher.ino: open it in the Arduino IDE, set Wi-Fi in config.h, upload

You never need to read the generated C, but it's plain and readable if you want to.

docs.title: The Python you can use
docs.text:
Nodes, tools, conditions and rules use the parts of Python that make sense on a microcontroller: if/elif/else, for i in range(n), comparisons, and/or/not, + - * // %, x if c else y, min/max/abs, local whole numbers and booleans, s.field = ..., calls to your other functions and to drivers, and lookup tables (POINTS[s.cam] with POINTS a dict at the top of the file). Not available: lists, strings other than Choice values and messages, floats, imports inside functions, while loops (they could hang the board) and recursion. Anything else stops the build with the file, line and what to use instead:

agent.py:131: floats aren't supported yet; use whole numbers (e.g. tenths of a degree)

Conditions and @rules may only read Choice and Think fields: the build checks the C against the Python (and trains the model, if any) on every combination of them, so their answers must not depend on memory or hardware.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Built in: LED, Buzzer, Servo, DigitalIn, Button, AnalogIn, Camera (snapshots served at /snapshot.jpg), Clock (internet time), Wifi, Phone (messages on the web page). On the PC they're simulated: set motion.value = True or clock.set(hour=22). The build stops if two drivers share a pin, or a pin belongs to the camera, flash or PSRAM.

For your own hardware, write the C and give Python a stand-in for the PC:

class Feeder(CDriver):
    c_files = ["feeder.c"]                  # void feeder_dispense(int32_t portions)
    def dispense(self, portions: int) -> None:
        print("feeding", portions)          # what happens on the PC

docs.title: Coming from LangGraph
docs.text: LangGraph tiny-langgraph TypedDict state class S(State) with Choice, Think, Int fields (fixed types: a C struct on the board) add_node, add_edge, add_conditional_edges, START, END the same compile(), invoke(), stream() the same get_graph().draw_mermaid() the same tools + ToolNode @tool(cost, achieves, needs, approval) + prebuilt.Act([...]) the LLM decides your @rules + the planner decide; optionally a tiny model trained on them proposes, and the verifier keeps it safe interrupt() + checkpointer prebuilt.ask / interrupt(); state.waiting, then app.resume(state, True) parallel branches not supported: one way out of each node

docs.title: Try the C side (no hardware needed)
docs.text:
make demo                 # examples, including the door guard with its on-device model
make trace                # writes build/door_guard.log

Open viewer/index.html in a browser, then Open log and pick build/door_guard.log (or just click Load demo). app.invoke(..., trace="run.log") writes the same format from Python.

docs.title: Lower level: schema.yaml and a C graph
docs.text:
The door guard (examples/door_guard) is written the other way: the agent described in schema.yaml (inputs, scores, rules, tools) and the graph written by hand in C. Use it when you want full control of the firmware.

scores:                     # points per observation, added up
  suspicion:
    tod:    { night: 2 }
    expect: { owner: -2, milkman: -2, courier: -2 }
rules:
  think:
    threat:                 # first matching rule wins
      - hi: visitor == hi and suspicion >= 3
      - lo: true
  want:
    informed_high: threat == hi

python tools/tlg.py check examples/door_guard/schema.yaml   # validate
python tools/tlg.py all   examples/door_guard/schema.yaml   # generate C, make data, train

static const tlg_node_t NODES[] = {
    [SENSE]  = { "sense",  sense,  TLG_EDGE(ASSESS) },
    [VERIFY] = { "verify", verify, TLG_ROUTE(after_verify, ACT, ASK, PLAN, FALLBACK) },
    ...
};

Graphs are static tables: no heap, nothing fails at runtime because memory ran out. Every route declares where it can go, so tlg_validate() catches broken graphs before they run. A paused run is plain data: save it and resume after a reboot (examples/plant_care).

docs.title: Trace viewer
docs.text:
Add the tracer to a graph (.on_step = tlg_trace_on_step) and every step becomes one line on the serial port: @tlg {"k":"step",...}. Your own prints can share the port.

viewer/index.html is one file with no dependencies. It lays out the graph, highlights the path of each run, shows the agent's notes per step, and replays runs step by step. In Chrome or Edge, Connect device reads a board over USB live.

docs.title: On the board, over Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Every sketch the build makes (and ports/arduino/door_guard_web) serves the viewer from the board itself: open http://pet-watcher.local on your phone and watch it think. When the agent wants to do something risky, the page asks you, and the approval needs a PIN.

Open the .ino in the Arduino IDE, set your Wi-Fi, PIN and time zone in config.h, upload. Without Wi-Fi the board starts its own network (page at http://192.168.4.1). For the door guard, python tools/arduino_bundle.py assembles build/arduino/door_guard_web.

  • Events reach the page by polling every half second, served from tlg_hub, a buffer of recent events that also keeps the graph, so a page opened later still has context.
  • Approvals also work with the BOOT button or by typing y/n in the Serial Monitor; no answer within 2 minutes counts as no.
  • The page is plain HTTP on your local network, read-only without the PIN, with a lockout after 5 wrong PINs. No cross-origin access, so other websites can't read the board.
  • No board? make fake-board serves the same web API on your PC from a recorded trace.

docs.title: Model vs planner-only on the chip
docs.text:
The pet watcher on an ESP32-S3-CAM, the same situations run both ways (USE_MODEL in examples/pet_watcher/agent.py switches between them):

With the model (float32) Planner only (default) Proposing a plan ~120 ms (119-145 ms) 40 µs Verifying it not recorded separately 36-38 µs Whole run, with Serial logging on ~132 ms ~12 ms, of which ~10 ms is printing Flash for the model weights 184,540 bytes 0 Whole sketch (camera, web viewer) 1,269,434 bytes flash, 76,884 bytes globals 1,080,826 bytes flash, 76,612 bytes globals Correct answers 388 / 388 held-out situations (it learned to copy @rules) all 3,888 (it is @rules + the planner)

For decisions that depend only on the current moment, rules + the planner are about 3,000 times faster than the model, need no model flash, and are right by construction. That's why planner-only is the default. The model has to earn its place by doing something the planner can't, such as deciding from the recent history of events; that's the next research step.

Also measured on the board, with the model: free heap stayed at ~181-188 KB over 28 runs (no leak), and the escalation worked: it chirped at the cat, then notified the owner once chirping stopped working.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text:
Door guard model 46,608 parameters, 186 KB (float32) Pet watcher model 46,128 parameters, 180 KB (float32) Accuracy on held-out situations door guard 1,843 / 1,843, pet watcher 388 / 388 exact answers Model decision time 0.4 ms on a PC, ~120 ms on the ESP32-S3 Code size on ESP32-S3 runtime 1.9 KB, planner + verifier 2.1 KB, tracer 1.3 KB, LM engine 2.6 KB Deepest stack use 1.4 KB (the planner) C and Python agree rules + planner on all 18,432 door guard and 3,888 pet watcher situations; the model engine (C vs numpy) on all 3,888 pet watcher situations

Fault injection (build/door_guard --corrupt N) damages N model weights on purpose. Up to about 20 damaged weights the model still answers correctly; beyond that it writes malformed output, which the agent discards, and the planner decides instead. No unsafe action ran at any level tested.

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
python/     tiny_langgraph: Python API, Python-to-C converter, build, schema toolchain
core/       graph runtime, planner + verifier, tracer, hub, agent bookkeeping (plain C11)
lm/         transformer inference engine                     (plain C11)
drivers/    built-in drivers: PC (prints) and ESP32-S3 (Arduino)
viewer/     trace viewer                                     (one HTML file)
ports/      arduino: board template with the Wi-Fi viewer; door_guard_web
tools/      tlg.py for schema.yaml agents, Arduino bundling, fake board
examples/   pet_watcher (Python agent + model), door_guard (schema.yaml + C graph + model),
            hello, plant_care (approval + checkpoint)
tests/      C unit tests, toolchain and Python API tests, C-vs-Python cross-checks

make check runs everything; CI runs it with gcc and clang, under sanitizers, and checks that the generated code and the committed model are up to date.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The model learns from rules you write, so today it can only be as good as your rules, and it's slower than running them: for decisions that depend only on the current moment it adds nothing over rules + the planner (see Results so far). It's optional for that reason; making it useful (learning from history) is research in progress.
  • Python on the device is a subset (no floats, lists or strings yet), and the inputs the model reads are categorical: turn measurements into Choice values in a node. Learning from a large LLM as the teacher is the next big step.
  • float32 only for now; int8 with ESP32-S3 SIMD is planned (the earlier, 4x larger model took about 0.5 s per decision on the chip, limited by memory bandwidth).
  • Up to 8 outcomes, 32 actions and 32 facts per schema; inputs are categorical.
  • The door guard's rules lower the threat when a visitor is expected, so an intruder arriving at delivery time looks less suspicious (demo scenario 8). It's a design weakness worth fixing in your own rules, kept visible on purpose.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
• [x] Graph runtime: edges, routes, cycles, interrupts, checkpoints, validation, Mermaid
  • [x] Planner + verifier generated from a schema
  • [x] Schema toolchain: generate, label, train, export
  • [x] Trace viewer: replay and live over USB
  • [x] ESP32-S3 port with a web viewer served by the board, and approvals from the page (Arduino)
  • [x] Python API like LangGraph; converted to C and checked against the Python automatically
  • [x] Built-in drivers (LED, buzzer, servo, inputs, camera, clock) and your own C drivers
  • [ ] ESP-IDF port; MQTT for remote access
  • [ ] int8 model + ESP32-S3 SIMD
  • [ ] Learning loop: log uncertain cases on the device, label them with a large LLM, retrain
  • [x] Model optional; planner-only by default
  • [ ] Benchmarks on hardware: latency and memory done for the pet watcher; energy per decision to do
  • [ ] A model that decides from the recent history of events (design in progress)
  • [ ] Verifier fuzzing

docs.title: Rules, planner, verifier
docs.text: How an agent decides, in three steps: rules say what's wanted, the planner finds how, and the verifier checks the plan before anything runs.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
goals = Goals(
    logged=1,                                   # weight 1
    fed=Goal(5, only_if_wanted=True),           # weight 5; never do it unless wanted
    told=Goal(3, only_if_wanted=True),
)
  • Weight (0–255) is how much a goal matters when not everything is possible.
  • only_if_wanted=True: a plan that achieves this goal when the rules didn't ask for it is rejected. Use it for anything with a side effect, like feeding or alarms.

Up to 32 goals per agent.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
@rules
def assess(s: Watcher):
    if s.meal == "due" and s.waiting == "no":
        if s.feeder_online == "yes":
            want(goals.fed)
        else:
            want(goals.told)
    if s.feed_reply == "refused":
        want(goals.told)

The @rules function runs every time. It calls want(...) and may set Think fields. It may only read Choice, Think and Score fields: no Int fields, no hardware, no note(). That way the build can check it on every situation.

docs.title: Planner
docs.text:
prebuilt.plan finds the plan with the highest total weight of wanted goals, and among those, the lowest cost. It only uses tools whose conditions (needs=) are true now, and keeps their order (after=).

Goals How it searches Memory up to 8 every combination (exact) ~1.25 KB of stack 9–32 a pruned exact search in a workspace ESP32-S3: 16,384 states (352 KB, PSRAM). NodeMCU: 1,024 states (22 KB) doesn't fit greedy (best weight per cost), noted in the trace none

The Python planner and the C planner match step for step, including tie-breaking, so the build can compare their answers.

docs.title: Verifier
docs.text:
prebuilt.verify checks a plan before anything runs. A plan fails if:

  • a tool's condition isn't true now: dispense needs may_feed
  • a tool comes before a goal it must follow
  • it achieves an only_if_wanted goal nobody asked for
  • it misses something the planner could achieve
  • it costs more than the planner's plan for the same goals
  • it uses a tool a human just refused

If a tool needs approval, the plan goes to ask first. If the plan fails, the graph replans. The verifier is plain rules that run in time proportional to the plan's length. A model may propose plans (Models), but the verifier always has the last word.

docs.title: Why not just an LLM?
docs.text: For decisions that depend only on the current moment, rules + the planner are right by construction and take microseconds. Measured on an ESP32-S3: planning ~40 µs and verifying ~37 µs, against ~120 ms for a tiny transformer that only learned to copy the rules. A model earns its place only where the planner can't reach. See Results and limitations.

docs.title: The graph
docs.text:
The same API as LangGraph's StateGraph.

graph = StateGraph(Feeder)
graph.add_node("sense", sense)
graph.add_node("assess", assess)
graph.add_node("plan", prebuilt.plan)
graph.add_node("verify", prebuilt.verify)
graph.add_node("ask", prebuilt.ask)
graph.add_node("act", prebuilt.Act([dispense, refuse]))
graph.add_edge(START, "sense")
graph.add_edge("sense", "assess")
graph.add_edge("assess", "plan")
graph.add_edge("plan", "verify")
graph.add_conditional_edges("verify", prebuilt.after_verify, ["act", "ask", "plan"])
graph.add_conditional_edges("ask", prebuilt.after_ask, ["verify", "plan"])
graph.add_edge("act", END)
app = graph.compile(name="feeder")

graph LR
  START((start)) --> sense --> assess --> plan --> verify
  verify -->|ok| act --> END((end))
  verify -->|needs approval| ask
  verify -->|wrong| plan
  ask -->|yes| verify
  ask -->|no| plan

app.get_graph().draw_mermaid() (or python agent.py mermaid) prints this diagram for your own graph.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text: A node is a function taking the state: def sense(s: Feeder): .... It runs on your PC as Python and on the board as the C the build converts it to, so it uses the Python you can use.

docs.title: Prebuilt nodes
docs.text: Node What it does @rules function decides Think fields and calls want(goals.x) prebuilt.plan the cheapest plan of tools for what's wanted prebuilt.reason a tiny transformer proposes the plan instead (optional; Models) prebuilt.verify checks the plan; routes with prebuilt.after_verify prebuilt.ask asks a human about risky tools; routes with prebuilt.after_ask prebuilt.Act([tools]) runs the plan's tools in order. The list order is fixed into a trained model's vocabulary. prebuilt.Classify({field: question}, model=...) a catalog model answers a Score field prebuilt.Mailbox(serves=..., uses=...) requests and replies from other boards; put it right after sense

docs.title: Routes
docs.text: add_conditional_edges(source, route, [targets]) takes every target the route can return. The graph refuses a route that can return something you didn't list, so a graph can't go somewhere unexpected on the board. Your own route functions return a node name as a string.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
s = Feeder()
app.invoke(s, verbose=True)            # one run; prints each step
for node, notes in app.stream(s): ...  # step by step
app.invoke(s, trace="run.log")         # a trace for the viewer
app.invoke(s, approve=lambda q: True)  # answer approvals in code

A run is one pass from START to END. On the board, the graph runs every RUN_EVERY_MS (30 s by default). Int fields keep their values between runs.

docs.title: Pausing for a human
docs.text:
app.invoke(s)
if s.waiting:                    # e.g. "approve dispense?"
    app.resume(s, True)          # or False

interrupt("question") in your own node pauses the same way. On the board, the question appears on the web page (PIN), and the BOOT button or y/n in the Serial Monitor answer it. No answer within 2 minutes counts as no.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: One way out of each node (no parallel branches), and at most max_steps=32 steps per run, so a loop can't hang the board.

docs.title: State and fields
docs.text:
The state is what the agent knows. Like a LangGraph TypedDict, but with fixed types: on the board it's a C struct.

class Pet(State):
    """watches the cat and feeds it"""              # one line about the agent (shown to MCP clients)
    cat          = Choice("none", "seen", "in_zone")
    meal         = Choice("not_due", "due", "overdue")
    mischief     = Think("no", "yes")
    unusual      = Score("no", "odd", "alarming")
    fed_at       = Int(-1000)

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
Type What it holds Who sets it Rules may read it Choice(*values, default=None) one of a few named values; the first is the default your nodes (usually sense) yes Think(*values) a conclusion your @rules (or a model, in a reason node) yes Score(*levels) ordered levels, lowest first a catalog model, through prebuilt.Classify yes Int(default=0) a whole number (int32): memory between runs, counters, timestamps your nodes and tools no

Values are lower_snake_case strings. Setting a value that isn't one of the field's values raises an error on the PC, so mistakes show up before you flash.

docs.title: Why rules can't read Int
docs.text:
The build checks your agent by running every combination of Choice, Think and Score values through both the C and the Python. That's only possible because those fields have a few values each. An Int has four billion, so rules and conditions may not read them. Turn a number into a Choice in a node instead:

def sense(s: Pet):
    s.fed_recently = "yes" if clock.minutes() - s.fed_at < 180 else "no"   # Int -> Choice

docs.title: Fields the framework fills
docs.text:
Some prebuilt nodes expect fields with specific names. The graph checks they exist, and if one is missing it prints the line to add:

Node Fields prebuilt.Mailbox(serves=[feed]) feed_asked = Choice("no", "yes"), feed_<param> = Choice(<its values>) prebuilt.Mailbox(uses={feeder: [feed]}) feeder_online = Choice("no", "yes"), feed_reply = Choice("none", <replies>) prebuilt.Classify({"unusual": ...}) unusual = Score(...)

docs.title: After a run
docs.text: s.plan the tool names that ran, e.g. ['dispense'] s.waiting the question, if the run paused for a human; otherwise None

docs.title: Tools and approvals
docs.text:
A tool is an action the planner may choose.

def may_feed(s: Feeder) -> bool:
    return s.feed_asked == "yes" and s.fed_recently == "no"

@tool(cost=3, achieves=[goals.fed, goals.answered], needs=may_feed)
def dispense(s: Feeder):
    led.blink(3, 200)
    s.fed_at = clock.minutes()
    mailbox.reply(feed, "done")

docs.title: @tool(...)
docs.text:
Argument Meaning cost 1–1000; the planner prefers cheap plans achieves the goal(s) it reaches: goals.fed or a list needs condition function(s) that must be true for it to be allowed after goal(s) that must be reached earlier in the plan approval True: a human approves before it runs

Up to 32 tools and 32 conditions per agent.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text: A condition is a named function of the state that returns True or False. Like rules, conditions may only read Choice, Think and Score fields. The verifier checks them on the board before every tool runs, whoever proposed the plan.

docs.title: The tool body
docs.text: The body is a node: drivers, memory (Int fields), note(...) for the trace, calls to other boards. Return nothing for success. Returning False marks the tool as failed: the rest of the plan doesn't run, and the trace says so.

docs.title: Approvals
docs.text:
@tool(cost=2, achieves=goals.alarmed, approval=True)
def sound_alarm(s: Door):
    siren.on()

When a plan contains an approval tool, the graph goes verify → ask:

  • yes: back to verify, then act
  • no: the tool is banned for this run, and the planner finds the best plan without it
Where How to answer PC app.invoke(s, approve=lambda q: True), or check s.waiting and call app.resume(s, True) Board web page Yes / No, with the PIN from config.h (locked for a minute after 5 wrong PINs) Board the BOOT (FLASH) button for yes, or y / n in the Serial Monitor

No answer within APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_MS (2 minutes) counts as no.

docs.title: Your first agent
docs.text: This page builds a small cat feeder for a NodeMCU. Press the button to ask for food; the feeder feeds unless it fed in the last 3 hours. The rule is enforced by the verifier, on the board as well as on your PC.

docs.title: The whole file
docs.text:
Save this as feeder.py:

from tiny_langgraph import START, END, Choice, Int, State, StateGraph, Goal, Goals, prebuilt, rules, tool, want
from tiny_langgraph.drivers import Button, Clock, LED

button, clock, led = Button(pin="D3"), Clock(), LED(pin="D4")

class Feeder(State):
    asked        = Choice("no", "yes")
    fed_recently = Choice("no", "yes")
    fed_at       = Int(-1000)                       # memory between runs

goals = Goals(fed=Goal(5, only_if_wanted=True))

def may_feed(s: Feeder) -> bool:                    # a condition: checked on the device too
    return s.fed_recently == "no"

@tool(cost=3, achieves=goals.fed, needs=may_feed)
def dispense(s: Feeder):
    led.blink(3, 200)
    s.fed_at = clock.minutes()

def sense(s: Feeder):                               # a node: plain Python
    s.asked = "yes" if button.pressed() else "no"
    s.fed_recently = "yes" if clock.minutes() - s.fed_at < 180 else "no"

@rules
def assess(s: Feeder):                              # what the agent wants
    if s.asked == "yes":
        want(goals.fed)

graph = StateGraph(Feeder)
graph.add_node("sense", sense)
graph.add_node("assess", assess)
graph.add_node("plan", prebuilt.plan)               # cheapest plan for what's wanted
graph.add_node("verify", prebuilt.verify)           # checked before anything runs
graph.add_node("ask", prebuilt.ask)                 # human approval for risky tools
graph.add_node("act", prebuilt.Act([dispense]))
graph.add_edge(START, "sense")
graph.add_edge("sense", "assess")
graph.add_edge("assess", "plan")
graph.add_edge("plan", "verify")
graph.add_conditional_edges("verify", prebuilt.after_verify, ["act", "ask", "plan"])
graph.add_conditional_edges("ask", prebuilt.after_ask, ["verify", "plan"])
graph.add_edge("act", END)
app = graph.compile(name="feeder")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.cli()                                       # python feeder.py check / build nodemcu

docs.title: What each part is
docs.text: Part What it is More Button, Clock, LED hardware, with your pins; simulated on the PC Drivers class Feeder(State) what the agent knows: observations (Choice) and memory (Int) State and fields Goals what the agent can achieve, with weights Rules, planner, verifier @tool an action: its cost, the goal it achieves, the condition it needs Tools and approvals sense a node that turns sensor readings into fields The graph @rules decides what's wanted in this situation Rules, planner, verifier prebuilt.plan/verify/ask/Act the ready-made nodes that plan, check, ask and act The graph

docs.title: Run it on your PC
docs.text:
import feeder
s = feeder.Feeder()
feeder.button.value = True          # simulate a press
feeder.app.invoke(s, verbose=True)
print(s.plan)                       # ['dispense']

Simulated outputs print what they would do (led > blink 3x 200 ms). Run it again straight away and the plan is empty: fed_recently is now "yes", so the condition may_feed blocks dispense.

docs.title: Check the C
docs.text:
python feeder.py check

check: the C decides exactly like your Python in all 4 situations

The build converts your nodes, tools, conditions and rules to C, compiles them, and runs every combination of the Choice fields through both the C and the Python. If they disagree anywhere, the build stops and shows the situation.

docs.title: Make the sketch
docs.text:
python feeder.py build nodemcu       # or: build esp32s3

This writes build/nodemcu/feeder/feeder.ino. Continue with Flash a board.

docs.title: Flash a board
docs.text: python agent.py build <board> makes a complete Arduino sketch in build/<board>/<name>/.

docs.title: 1. Edit config.h
docs.text:
The build writes config.h once and never overwrites it, so your settings survive rebuilds.

Setting What it is WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD your Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz). Empty: the board starts its own network, page at http://192.168.4.1 HOSTNAME the page is at http://<hostname>.local APPROVAL_PIN needed to approve risky tools from the web page (made up at build time) TIMEZONE a POSIX TZ string, e.g. "PKT-5", "CET-1CEST,M3.5.0,M10.5.0/3" RUN_EVERY_MS how often the graph runs (default 30 s; 0 = only when you type r) SERIAL_LOG 0 prints one summary line per run (for timing) LOG_DAYS days of data log kept on the flash NET_KEY boards that talk to each other need the same key (Multi-agent) MCP_KEY the key AI clients send (MCP server)

docs.title: 2. Tools menu
docs.text:
The build prints the exact settings for your board. For reference:

ESP32-S3NodeMCU (ESP8266) Setting Value Board ESP32S3 Dev Module Flash Size 16MB PSRAM OPI PSRAM Partition Scheme 16M Flash (3MB APP/9.9MB FATFS) Setting Value Board NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module) Flash Size 4MB (FS:2MB OTA:~1019KB) Upload Speed 115200 is the most reliable

docs.title: 3. Upload and watch
docs.text:
Upload, open the Serial Monitor at 115200, and press reset:

tiny-langgraph: feeder on nodemcu
joining Wi-Fi "my-wifi".......
open  http://192.168.1.47/   or   http://feeder.local/
MCP:  http://192.168.1.47/mcp   2 tools, key in config.h (MCP_KEY)
free heap: 8984 bytes

[run 1]
    inputs: asked=no fed_recently=no
    want: nothing
    planner: (nothing) (cost 0)
  -> done after 6 steps (planner 119 us, verify 97 us, run 11.69 ms, free heap 8656)

In the Serial Monitor, r runs the graph now, and y/n answer a pending approval.

docs.title: 4. Open the page
docs.text: Open the address it printed. The page shows every run live: the graph, the path taken, what was wanted, the plan, and why. See Web page and trace viewer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Needed for Python 3.9+ writing and running agents A C compiler (gcc or clang) optional: checking the C against your Python on the PC. Without one, that check is skipped (CI always runs it). Arduino IDE with the ESP32 or ESP8266 board package putting an agent on a board PyTorch optional: only to train the tiny transformer

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
tiny-langgraph isn't on PyPI yet. Install it from the repository:

git clone https://github.com/mak-ahoy/tiny-langgraph
cd tiny-langgraph
pip install -e .                 # numpy, pyyaml
pip install -e ".[train]"        # optional: adds torch, to train a model

Check it works:

cd examples/pet_watcher
python agent.py

You should see the agent run a few situations on your PC, with simulated hardware.

docs.title: Board packages for the Arduino IDE
docs.text:
In File → Preferences → Additional boards manager URLs, add whichever you need:

https://espressif.github.io/arduino-esp32/package_esp32_index.json
https://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json

Then install esp32 and/or esp8266 in Tools → Board → Boards Manager.

Windows: NodeMCU upload fails with 'A device attached to the system is not functioning'

Many NodeMCU boards use a clone CH340 USB chip, and newer CH340 drivers (3.8 and later) don't work with it. Install driver 3.4.2014.8. In Device Manager, right-click the CH340 device → Update driver → Let me pick, and choose 3.4. If uploads then time out at Connecting..., hold FLASH, tap RST, and release FLASH.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py"
make check          # Linux/macOS: the C tests, examples, sanitizers and everything above

docs.title: Boards
docs.text:
python agent.py build esp32s3     # default
python agent.py build nodemcu
python agent.py build c           # just the C files, for your own firmware
ESP32-S3 NodeMCU (ESP8266) RAM 320 KB + 8 MB PSRAM 80 KB (~9–40 KB free, depending on the agent) Flash 16 MB 4 MB Agent runs in its own task (the web page stays responsive) in loop() Planner workspace (more than 8 goals) 16,384 states in PSRAM 1,024 states Tiny transformer (prebuilt.reason) yes no: not enough RAM Camera ESP32-S3-EYE and XIAO ESP32S3 pin maps no Data log FFat, 30 days by default LittleFS, 10 days Measured plan + verify ~40 + ~37 µs ~120 + ~100 µs

docs.title: Pins
docs.text:
Use the board's own pin names: GPIO numbers on the ESP32-S3, and "D0"…"D8", "A0" on a NodeMCU. The build checks the pins against the board and stops with an explanation if something can't work:

Check Example two drivers on one pin stops a pin used by USB, flash, PSRAM or the camera stops pulldown=True on a NodeMCU pin other than D0 stops: add a 10 kΩ resistor to GND instead analog input on a NodeMCU pin other than A0 stops a NodeMCU boot pin (D3, D4, D8) a warning: fine as an input, but it mustn't be held LOW (D8: HIGH) while the board starts

docs.title: Free memory on the NodeMCU
docs.text: The sketch prints free heap at boot and after every run. The NodeMCU needs a few KB free for Wi-Fi and web requests. The two-board feeder example has ~9 KB free: enough, but tight.

docs.title: Your own firmware
docs.text: build c writes plain C11 (<name>_agent.c/.h, <name>_rules.c and the runtime) with drivers behind tlg_drivers.h. See C runtime.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
Create hardware at the top of your agent file, with your pins, and use it in nodes and tools. On the PC, outputs print what they would do and inputs return whatever you set.

from tiny_langgraph.drivers import LED, Buzzer, Servo, DigitalIn, Button, AnalogIn, Camera, Clock, Wifi, Phone

light  = LED(pin=21)
motion = DigitalIn(pin=12, pulldown=True)
feeder = Servo(pin=13)
clock  = Clock()

docs.title: Built in
docs.text:
Driver Methods On the PC LED(pin, active_low=False) on(), off(), blink(times, ms) prints Buzzer(pin) beep(ms), tone(hz, ms) prints Servo(pin) turn(angle) prints DigitalIn(pin, pullup=False, pulldown=False, active_low=False) read() -> bool motion.value = True Button(pin=0) pressed() -> bool (to GND, like BOOT) button.value = True AnalogIn(pin) read() -> int (0..4095) sensor.value = 2048 Camera(model="esp32s3_eye") snapshot() -> bool, served at /snapshot.jpg Clock() hour(), minutes() (internet time on the board) clock.set(hour=22, minutes=...) Wifi() connected() -> bool Phone() send(text): a message on the board's web page prints

drivers.quiet() stops the PC printing.

docs.title: Your own hardware
docs.text:
Write the C, and give Python a stand-in for the PC:

from tiny_langgraph.drivers import CDriver

class Feeder(CDriver):
    c_files = ["feeder.c"]              # next to your agent file
    def dispense(self, portions: int) -> None:
        print("feeding", portions)      # what happens on the PC

hopper = Feeder()

/* feeder.c: functions named <prefix>_<method>; prefix = the class name in lower case */
#include <stdint.h>
void feeder_init(void) { /* optional: runs once at startup */ }
void feeder_dispense(int32_t portions) { /* drive your motor */ }

Methods take and return whole numbers or booleans.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
Every board serves the Model Context Protocol at http://<board>/mcp, so AI clients like Claude Code can list a board's tools and call them.

The client only asks. An MCP call enters the board's mailbox like a request from another board, the agent runs, its rules and verifier decide, and the reply is the tool's result.

docs.title: Tools a board offers
docs.text: Tool What it is one per served contract, e.g. feed parameters as string enums (portions: one/two), the replies as the output schema <board>_status read-only: the board's current fields and its last plan

docs.title: Connect Claude Code
docs.text:
claude mcp add --transport http feeder http://192.168.1.47/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer <MCP_KEY>"

MCP_KEY is in the board's config.h; the build makes up a random one. Then, in a new session:

Ask the feeder to feed the cat one portion.

The answer is done, or refused if the feeder's rule says it was fed recently.

docs.title: Without a board
docs.text:
cd examples/feeding_station
python serve.py          # the feeder on http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp, key "feeder-demo"

McpServer in Python answers exactly like the board's C (the tests send both the same session):

from tiny_langgraph.net import McpServer
McpServer(endpoint, key="secret", about="Feeds the cat").serve(8765)

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Transport Streamable HTTP: JSON-RPC 2.0 POST /mcp, plain JSON answers Methods initialize, notifications, ping, tools/list, tools/call Protocol versions 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26, 2024-11-05 Waiting a call waits up to MCP_WAIT_MS (10 s) for the board's answer. On the ESP32 it answers busy while the board waits for a human approval. On the NodeMCU the agent runs during the request. Fingerprints in _meta.tiny_langgraph of each tool, so another PC can import the contract

Local network only

Plain HTTP with a bearer key: the key travels unencrypted. Keep the board on your own network.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Models in tiny-langgraph fill state fields; they never pick actions. Your rules read the fields like any other, and the verifier checks every plan, so a model can't make the agent do something your rules and conditions forbid. Every model's C is checked against its Python at build time.

docs.title: The catalog: prebuilt.Classify
docs.text:
from tiny_langgraph import Score, models, prebuilt

class Room(State):
    seen    = Choice("no", "yes")
    tod     = Choice("day", "night")
    unusual = Score("no", "odd", "alarming")      # answered by a model
    risk    = Score("low", "high")

def active(s: Room) -> bool:
    return s.seen == "yes"

NOTICE = models.Counting(active=active, clock=clock)
RISK   = models.Tree(reads=["tod", "unusual"], max_depth=3)

graph.add_node("notice", prebuilt.Classify({"unusual": "Is the activity unusual for this room?"}, model=NOTICE))
graph.add_node("risk",   prebuilt.Classify({"risk": "Is this worth an alert?"}, model=RISK))

Then your rules react: if s.unusual == "alarming": want(goals.alerted).

docs.title: models.Counting: what's normal here
docs.text:
Learns how active a place usually is at each hour of the day, from your own data, and flags what isn't normal.

Argument Meaning active a condition: is something happening this run? clock your Clock() driver checks any of "quiet" (nothing for unusually long), "busy" (much more than usual), "slow" (a slow day) odd probability below which a moment is odd (0 < odd < 0.1, default 0.05) false_alarms_per_week the alarm threshold is picked from your normal days to stay within this (default 1)

It answers a Score with 2 levels (no, yes) or 3 (no, odd, alarming). Fit it on two weeks or more of normal days from the board's data log:

from tiny_langgraph.datalog import load_log, samples
rows = load_log("log.csv")                       # downloaded from the board's web page
NOTICE.fit(samples(rows, Room, active))
NOTICE.save("notice.json")                       # later: models.Counting(...).load("notice.json")

In our experiments on simulated cats, this beat a small transformer at spotting unusual days.

docs.title: models.Tree: a decision tree
docs.text:
RISK.fit([({"tod": "night", "unusual": "alarming"}, "high"), ...])    # (values, label) rows

It reads Choice/Score fields and answers a Choice or Score. The build checks the C on every combination of its inputs.

docs.title: The tiny transformer: prebuilt.reason
docs.text:
A reason node replaces plan with a small transformer (~46k parameters) trained on your @rules and the planner. The build trains it if PyTorch is installed (~1.5 min on a laptop CPU), and retrains only when the rules or tools change.

graph.add_node("reason", prebuilt.reason)
graph.add_edge("assess", "reason")
graph.add_edge("reason", "verify")

Writing is guided: at each step the model may only pick tools the verifier would allow, and the verifier keeps a model plan only if it's at least as good as the planner's.

When is it worth it?

For decisions that depend only on the current moment, it adds nothing: on an ESP32-S3 it takes ~120 ms where the planner takes 40 µs, for the same answers. In our planning experiments it won only for very busy agents, where the board can't search all plans (~30 goals wanted at once: 99.8% optimal vs 88.6%). ESP32-S3 only.

docs.title: Multi-agent
docs.text:
Boards advertise what they can do and ask each other for it, over ESP-NOW: no router needed, ESP32 and ESP8266 together, messages up to 250 bytes.

A call is a request, never a command. It arrives in the receiver's state as input fields. The receiver's own rules decide, its verifier checks the plan, and a tool replies.

docs.title: A contract
docs.text:
Both boards import the same contract:

# contracts.py
from tiny_langgraph import Contract

feed = Contract("feed", about="Give the cat food",
                params={"portions": ("one", "two")},
                replies=("done", "refused", "busy"))

Parameters and replies are small sets of values, like Choice fields, so both boards' builds can check every call. Each contract has a fingerprint (a hash of its name, parameters and replies) baked into both builds. A board with a different version of the contract counts as offline for it, and the trace says why.

docs.title: The board that serves it
docs.text:
mailbox = prebuilt.Mailbox(serves=[feed])

class Feeder(State):
    feed_asked    = Choice("no", "yes")        # filled by the mailbox
    feed_portions = Choice("one", "two")
    fed_recently  = Choice("no", "yes")

@tool(cost=3, achieves=[goals.fed, goals.answered], needs=may_feed)
def dispense(s: Feeder):
    feeder_motor.turn(90)
    mailbox.reply(feed, "done")

@tool(cost=1, achieves=goals.answered, needs=was_asked)
def refuse(s: Feeder):
    mailbox.reply(feed, "refused")

graph.add_node("mailbox", mailbox)             # right after sense

docs.title: The board that uses it
docs.text:
feeder  = Peer("feeder")                       # the other agent's name
mailbox = prebuilt.Mailbox(uses={feeder: [feed]})

class Watcher(State):
    feeder_online = Choice("no", "yes")        # filled by the mailbox
    feed_reply    = Choice("none", "done", "refused", "busy")

def feeder_up(s: Watcher) -> bool:
    return s.feeder_online == "yes"

@tool(cost=2, achieves=goals.fed, needs=feeder_up)
def ask_feeder(s: Watcher):
    feeder.call(feed, "one")

Sending is a tool like any other, so the planner chooses it and the verifier checks it. Here it's only allowed while the feeder is online. A board can serve and use contracts at the same time.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
online the peer announced itself (every 5 s) within the last 15 s, with matching fingerprints a request handled on the receiver's next run; dropped after 3 runs with no answer a reply arrives on the caller's next run, in <contract>_reply queues 4 requests per served contract, 2 replies per used contract

Only the reply to the latest call counts: if you ask twice, the first reply is dropped as stale.

docs.title: Try it on your PC
docs.text:
from tiny_langgraph import Network
net = Network()
net.board("watcher", watcher.app, watcher.Watcher())
net.board("feeder", feeder.app, feeder.Feeder())
net.run(verbose=True)          # one round: every board runs once, messages delivered
net.unplug("feeder")           # and net.plug("feeder")

examples/feeding_station/run.py plays a whole story. The tests also link both boards' generated C into one program and check it tells the same story byte for byte.

docs.title: On the boards
docs.text:
Both boards need the same NET_KEY in config.h and the same Wi-Fi channel: join the same router, or no router at all. The boot line shows the channel:

network: ESP-NOW as "watcher" on Wi-Fi channel 13 (boards must share the channel and NET_KEY)

docs.title: Boards built on different PCs
docs.text:
python -m tiny_langgraph.net export contracts.py feeder.contracts.json    # on the feeder's PC
python -m tiny_langgraph.net import feeder.contracts.json contracts.py    # on the other PC
python -m tiny_langgraph.net import http://feeder.local/mcp contracts.py --key <MCP_KEY>   # from a live board

Fingerprints are checked on import.

Not encrypted yet

Messages are ESP-NOW broadcasts filtered by a hash of NET_KEY. Anyone in radio range who knows the key can send requests. The receiving board's rules still decide what it does. Per-pair encryption is planned.

docs.title: On the board
docs.text:
Every sketch serves a live view of the agent from the board itself. Open http://<hostname>.local, or the IP printed at boot, on any phone or PC on the same network.

  • the graph, with each run's path highlighted
  • the agent's notes for each step: inputs, what's wanted, the plan, the verifier's verdict, what ran
  • approvals: Yes / No with the PIN
  • the data log: download it as CSV, or clear it (PIN)
  • /snapshot.jpg: the last camera picture, if the agent has a camera

The page is read-only without the PIN, and it's plain HTTP on your local network. Other websites can't read the board.

Endpoint GET /tlg/events?since=N trace lines GET /tlg/pending, POST /tlg/answer approvals GET /tlg/log.csv the data log (?day=2026-11-09 for one day) POST /mcp the MCP server

docs.title: The trace viewer on your PC
docs.text:
viewer/index.html is one file with no dependencies. Open it in a browser, then:

  • Open log: a trace written by app.invoke(s, trace="run.log") or by the C examples
  • Connect device (Chrome/Edge): read a board live over USB, with SERIAL_TRACE 1 in config.h
  • Load demo: a recorded door guard run

Trace lines look like @tlg {"k":"step",...} and can share the serial port with your own prints.

docs.title: The data log
docs.text: Once the board's clock is synced, every run appends one line to a file per day: time, every Choice/Score field, and the plan. The last LOG_DAYS days are kept. Download the log from the page to fit models on your PC.

docs.title: C runtime and schema.yaml
docs.text:
Under the Python API is a small C11 runtime you can also use directly.

core/tlg the graph: static node tables, edges, routes, interrupts, checkpoints, validation core/tlg_plan the planner and verifier core/tlg_trace, tlg_hub trace lines, and the buffer the web page reads core/tlg_net messages between boards (contracts, mailbox, announcements) core/tlg_mcp the MCP endpoint core/tlg_count models.Counting lm/tlg_lm the transformer inference engine (float32) drivers/ tlg_drivers.h, with PC (prints) and Arduino implementations

docs.title: A graph in C
docs.text:
static const tlg_node_t NODES[] = {
    [SENSE]  = { "sense",  sense,  TLG_EDGE(ASSESS) },
    [VERIFY] = { "verify", verify, TLG_ROUTE(after_verify, ACT, ASK, PLAN, FALLBACK) },
    ...
};
  • No heap: graphs are static tables, so nothing fails at runtime because memory ran out.
  • Every route declares where it can go, so tlg_validate() catches broken graphs before they run.
  • A paused run is plain data (tlg_run_t): save it and resume after a reboot (examples/plant_care).
make demo      # hello, plant_care, and the door guard with its on-device model
make trace     # build/door_guard.log, for the viewer

docs.title: schema.yaml
docs.text:
The door guard (examples/door_guard) is written the lower-level way: the agent's inputs, scores, rules and tools in schema.yaml, and the graph by hand in C.

scores:                     # points per observation, added up
  suspicion:
    tod:    { night: 2 }
    expect: { owner: -2, milkman: -2, courier: -2 }
rules:
  think:
    threat:                 # first matching rule wins
      - hi: visitor == hi and suspicion >= 3
      - lo: true
  want:
    informed_high: threat == hi

python tools/tlg.py check examples/door_guard/schema.yaml   # validate
python tools/tlg.py all   examples/door_guard/schema.yaml   # generate C, make data, train

docs.title: Coming from LangGraph
docs.text: LangGraph tiny-langgraph TypedDict state class S(State) with Choice, Think, Score, Int fields: fixed types, a C struct on the board add_node, add_edge, add_conditional_edges, START, END the same compile(), invoke(), stream() the same get_graph().draw_mermaid() the same tools + ToolNode @tool(cost, achieves, needs, after, approval) + prebuilt.Act([...]) the LLM decides what to call your @rules say what's wanted; the planner picks the tools; the verifier checks interrupt() + checkpointer prebuilt.ask / interrupt(); state.waiting, then app.resume(state, True) multi-agent, subgraphs agents on different boards, talking through contracts (Multi-agent) tools exposed over MCP every board is an MCP server (MCP server) parallel branches not supported: one way out of each node any Python a subset that converts to C (The Python you can use)

docs.title: What's different, and why
docs.text:
• No LLM in the loop by default. A microcontroller can't hold one. Your rules are the "reasoning", and they're checked exhaustively at build time.
  • Every decision is verifiable. The verifier runs on the device before any tool, whoever proposed the plan.
  • Everything is fixed at build time: the fields, tools, goals and contracts. That's what lets the build prove the C behaves like your Python.

docs.title: The Python you can use
docs.text:
Nodes, tools, conditions and rules run on the board as C, so they use the parts of Python that make sense on a microcontroller. Anything else stops the build with the file, the line, and what to use instead:

agent.py:131: floats aren't supported yet; use whole numbers (e.g. tenths of a degree)

docs.title: Supported
docs.text: Example if / elif / else for i in range(...), break, continue for i in range(3): buzzer.beep(100) return setting fields, += s.count += 1 local whole numbers and booleans late = clock.hour() >= 22 comparisons, in a tuple s.cat in ("seen", "in_zone") and, or, not + - * // % // and % round like Python, also for negative numbers x if c else y s.tod = "night" if h >= 22 else "day" min, max, abs calls to your other functions that take s if may_feed(s): ... driver methods servo.turn(90) lookup tables indexed by a Choice field POINTS[s.cam], with POINTS = {...} at the top of the file note("message", values...) a line in the trace want(goals.x) in @rules only interrupt("question") pause for a human peer.call(contract, "value"), mailbox.reply(contract, "value") Multi-agent; values are checked at build time

docs.title: Not supported (yet)
docs.text: Instead floats whole numbers: tenths of a degree, milliseconds lists and dicts at runtime Int fields; lookup tables at the top of the file strings other than Choice values and literal messages Choice fields while loops for i in range(n): a loop that can't hang the board recursion, lambdas, keyword arguments, imports inside functions

docs.title: Rules and conditions
docs.text: @rules functions and conditions (needs=) may only read Choice, Think and Score fields: no Int fields, no hardware, no note(). The build runs them on every combination of those fields. See State and fields.

docs.title: Limits per agent
docs.text: 32 goals, 32 tools, 32 conditions; up to 256 tokens in a trained model's vocabulary.

docs.title: Results and limitations
docs.text: All numbers below were measured on real boards unless marked otherwise.

docs.title: Model vs planner on the ESP32-S3
docs.text:
The pet watcher on an ESP32-S3-CAM, the same situations run both ways:

Tiny transformer (float32) Planner only (default) Proposing a plan ~120 ms (119–145 ms) 40 µs Verifying it included 36–38 µs Whole run, with Serial logging ~132 ms ~12 ms (~10 ms of it is printing) Flash for the model 184,540 bytes 0 Correct answers 388 / 388 held out (it learned to copy the rules) all 3,888 (it is the rules + planner)

For decisions that depend only on the current moment, rules + the planner are ~3,000× faster and right by construction, so planner-only is the default. Free heap stayed at ~181–188 KB over 28 runs (no leak).

docs.title: Two boards and MCP
docs.text: Boards watcher on an ESP32-S3, feeder on a NodeMCU, ESP-NOW on Wi-Fi channel 13 Story the watcher asks → the feeder feeds → asked again, it refuses by its own rule → the watcher tells the owner NodeMCU run 11.7 ms (planner 119 µs, verify 97 µs) ESP32-S3 run ~12 ms (planner ~33 µs, verify ~20 µs) MCP over Wi-Fi (NodeMCU) 0.3–0.5 s per call; Claude Code connects

docs.title: Planning experiments (PC, synthetic agents)
docs.text:
Agent Board's planner Tiny transformer (guided) 32 goals, ~22 wanted at once NodeMCU 86%, ESP32-S3 99% optimal 99.8% 32 goals, ~30 wanted at once 88.6% on both boards 99.8%

Guided writing (only tools the verifier would allow) made every model plan safe. The model earns its place only for very busy agents, and only together with the planner and the verifier.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• A Python subset on the device: no floats, lists or strings yet; inputs are categorical.
  • Hardware tested so far: one ESP32-S3-CAM and one NodeMCU.
  • Board-to-board messages aren't encrypted yet; MCP is plain HTTP with a bearer key.
  • The transformer is float32 and ESP32-S3 only; an int8 engine isn't built yet.
  • Up to 32 goals, 32 tools, 32 conditions per agent.

docs.text:
